title: Pot Odds, Equity and Expected Value
intro: Every decision in poker comes down to one question: which action wins the most on average? This page gives the arithmetic for answering it: pot odds, expected value, implied and reverse implied odds, fold equity, and the thresholds every bet size sets for both the bettor and the caller.

blocks.text: Pot odds

Pot odds compare what a call costs with what it can win. If the pot holds 100 and an opponent bets 50, you call 50 to win the 150 already in the middle: odds of 150 to 50, or 3 to 1. Put as a percentage, the call is 50 of the final pot of 200, so you need to win more than 25% of the time for the call to pay. That percentage is the break-even equity:

blocks.caption: Here $p$ is the pot before the bet and $b$ the bet. A half-pot bet needs 25%, a pot-sized bet 33%, a bet of twice the pot 40%.

blocks.text: Compare that number with your equity (see #/games/poker/probability). With a flush draw on the turn, 9 outs give 19.6%; facing a half-pot bet that needs 25%, the call loses money on this card alone. To express the same comparison in odds, as many players do: the draw is about 4.1 to 1 against and the pot offers 3 to 1.
Expected value

The expected value (EV) of an action is the sum, over every way things can turn out, of the chance of each outcome times what you win or lose in it. Measured from the moment of decision, folding is worth 0 (money already in the pot is no longer yours: thinking otherwise is the sunk-cost mistake of being pot committed for the wrong reason). A call of $b$ into a pot that, with the bet, holds $P$ is worth

blocks.caption: where $e$ is your equity. It is zero exactly at $e = b/(P + b)$, the required equity above.

blocks.text: A play with positive EV (+EV) gains money on average, and one with negative EV (-EV) loses it. The aim is not to win the pot, but to choose the action with the highest EV. A fold can be the best play and so can a call that loses most of the time.

params.label: implied odds: more won later when you hit (bb)

blocks.text: The line crosses zero at the break-even equity. Adding implied odds moves the crossing to the left: a hand that is behind now can call if it will win more later.
Implied odds and reverse implied odds

Pot odds count only the money in the pot now. Implied odds count what you expect to win on later streets when you hit. Set-mining (calling with a small pair to try to flop a set) is the classic case: a set comes about one time in 8.5, so the call is only good if, when it hits, you will usually win at least 7.5 times the call from the opponent's stack. A common rule of thumb is to set-mine only when the effective stacks are at least 15 to 20 times the price of the call.

Reverse implied odds are the opposite: when your hand improves but loses a big pot to a better hand, or when it wins only small pots and loses big ones. A low flush draw against a higher one, or a weak ace that makes top pair with a poor kicker, has reverse implied odds. Hands that make the nuts have good implied odds; hands that make second-best hands have poor ones.
Fold equity and the semi-bluff

When you bet, an opponent may fold. The share of the pot you win that way is fold equity. A bet with a draw, such as a flush draw, is a semi-bluff: it can win at once when they fold, and when they call it still has equity to make the best hand. Its EV combines the two:

blocks.tex: EV(\text{bet}) = f \cdot p + (1 - f) \left[ e \cdot (p + 2b) - b \right]
blocks.caption: $f$ is how often they fold, $p$ the pot before the bet, $b$ the bet, and $e$ your equity when called (ignoring later betting).

blocks.text: A pure bluff with no equity ($e = 0$) is a bet of $b$ to win $p$. It shows a profit when the opponent folds more often than

blocks.caption: the bluff's break-even fold frequency, called alpha. A half-pot bluff must work 33% of the time, a pot-sized one 50%.

blocks.text: The defender's side: minimum defence frequency

Turn the last formula round. If the defender folds more than $\alpha$, every bluff shows a profit and the bettor can bluff with any two cards. To stop that, the defender has to continue (call or raise) at least

blocks.caption: the minimum defence frequency: 67% of the range against a half-pot bet, 50% against a pot-sized bet.

blocks.text: MDF is a guide, not a law. It assumes the bettor could hold any hand, and against a player who never bluffs the right defence frequency is far lower. But it is a useful check: if you fold 80% of your range to a half-pot bet, a thinking opponent will notice. The ideas of $\alpha$, MDF and the caller's required equity come together in game-theory optimal play, on #/games/poker/game-theory.

Three curves, one bet size: how often a pure bluff of that size must work ($\alpha$), how much of their range a defender must continue with (MDF), and how much equity a caller needs. As bets get larger the bluff needs more folds, the defender may fold more and a caller needs more equity. Rake raises both the bluffer's and the caller's thresholds and lowers the defence a bettor can demand: some of every pot is gone.
Stacks, commitment and rake

items: Effective stack: the smaller of the two stacks in a heads-up confrontation, since nobody can win more than the smaller stack from the other. Every stack-depth idea uses it.

Stack-to-pot ratio (SPR): the effective stack divided by the pot on the flop. With a low SPR (below about 3) top pair is usually strong enough to get all in; with a high SPR (above about 10) it often is not, and hands that make the nuts gain value.
Pot committed: so much of a stack is already in the pot that the remaining call is profitable with almost any equity. The reason is the pot odds, not the money already spent.

Rake: the house's fee, usually a percentage of each pot up to a cap. In small-stakes games it is often the biggest single cost a player faces and turns many marginal +EV calls into -EV ones. Rakeback returns part of it to players.

blocks.text: Expected value over many decisions

Because EV adds up, a player can treat poker as a long series of small bets, each with its own EV. Over enough hands the total result converges on the sum of the EVs; how many hands that takes is the subject of #/games/poker/variance-and-bankroll. All-in adjusted EV (or EV-adjusted winnings) replaces the actual result of each all-in hand with its expected value at the moment the money went in, which strips out the luck of how the board ran.

blocks.title: Calling with a flush draw
blocks.text: On the turn the pot is 60 bb. Your opponent bets 30 bb and you hold a nut flush draw with 9 outs and nothing else. Is the call profitable on pot odds alone? How much more would you need to win on the river when you hit to make it break even?
blocks.hint: Required equity is the call over the final pot. For the second part, set the EV with implied winnings $I$ to zero.
solution: Required equity: $30 / (60 + 30 + 30) = 25\%$. Your equity is $9/46 \approx 19.6\%$, so on pot odds alone the call loses.
With implied winnings $I$: $EV = 0.196 \times (90 + I) - 0.804 \times 30$. This is zero when $90 + I = 24.1 / 0.196 \approx 123$, so $I \approx 33$ bb.
You need to win about 33 bb more on average when the flush comes, which is plausible if stacks are deep and the opponent will pay off a river bet.
blocks.answer: no on pot odds alone; it breaks even if you win about 33 bb more when you hit

blocks.title: Bluff or not
blocks.text: On the river the pot is 40 bb. You have missed your draw and have no showdown value. You think the opponent will fold to a 30 bb bet 45% of the time. Should you bluff?
blocks.hint: Compare the fold frequency with $\alpha = b/(p+b)$, or compute EV directly.
solution: $\alpha = 30 / (40 + 30) \approx 42.9\%$. They fold 45%, a little more, so the bluff shows a small profit.
Directly: $EV = 0.45 \times 40 - 0.55 \times 30 = 18 - 16.5 = +1.5$ bb. Checking gives up and wins 0 (you can't win a showdown).

blocks.title: Defending against a pot bet
blocks.text: On the river your opponent bets the size of the pot. What share of your range must you continue with so that their bluffs can't profit automatically? What equity does a call need?
blocks.hint: Use MDF $= p/(p+b)$ and required equity $= b/(p+2b)$ with $b = p$.
solution: Required equity $= p/(3p) \approx 33\%$: a bluff-catcher should call if the bettor is bluffing at least a third of the time.
blocks.answer: continue with 50%; a call needs 33% equity
